fragments.text: Hi, my name is Adam White and I'm a professor at the University of Alberta. I work as a scientific director at AMI and I also work at Stratocool. Today I'd like to talk to you about what I call the future of automated decision making. And this is the idea that we can move machine learning and AI methods out into the real world. And the way we're going to do this is we're going to focus on a particular technology called Reinforced Learning and we're going to focus on a specific domain which is industrial control. So let's see how far we can get in 10 minutes. So like I said, I work in reinforcement learning

and I think this is key to making this happen. So what is reinforcement learning? Reinforcement learning actually comes from psychology where animals learn by trial and error interaction world. In fact, so do people. And this is basically the idea that you do some things, you see what gives good payoffs, good consequences and then you do those things more when you're in those situations again. And so the key kind of aspect of this is that this is a type of learning that the agent for itself can tell when it's right or wrong. This is different than classical supervised learning where people provide the labels. People say that's a cat, that's a dog, that's a hot dog.

And reinforcement learning the agent figures out on its own if what it's doing is working well or what it's doing is working up poorly. And as you can see in the little diagram there, reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning and more broadly, artificial intelligence. So of course, Reinforce Learning has had some really nice successes, and maybe going backwards to the slide here, many of you have probably heard about AlphaGo, where a Reinforce Learning program written by DeepMind played better Go than the World Champion in Go. Maybe more practically, the animation on the top there you can see is controlling a fusion reactor. And so this is an actual interesting problem where they train this thing in simulation and actually control the real fusion reactor and

of course the Atari game simulator where the famous DQN agent learned how to play Atari games better than people can. And so when I think about taking the next steps here, I think about what does it mean to apply reinforcement learning to something like water treatment or an industrial control problem? And so here I'm drawing the typical interaction diagram that we see in reinforcement course-learning, you have an agent and it's continually interacting with the world. And so the interaction just goes in a loop and goes on and on and on forever. The agent makes decisions, those decisions affect the world, which then causes the agent to perceive the changes in the world through its sensation.

And of course the world also gives a numerical feedback signal called the reward. And this is modeled just after our daily life. We might do things and those things have consequences in the world and we get feedback signals from the world. I touched a hot stove and it hurts, so that's the negative reward I would get, or I made a bunch of people happy by doing a good job in this talk, and then I get a bunch of positive feedback from people, so that's a positive reward for me. So punishing bad behavior, rewarding good behavior, so that the system can learn. Unfortunately, this picture is still a cartoon in the sense that we're not really widely

deploying these methods in the real world. We use them in simulations, but we don't use them much in the real world. And so one of the chief reasons for this is these systems are not sample efficient. They don't learn as fast as you or I do, or even basic animals. And so let's just take Atari, for example. The agent trains in each game for roughly a month, playing 24-7 at 60 frames per second in every single Atari game. I'd imagine that if I gave you an Atari game that you'd never seen before, you would probably learn to play it much faster than that. Because these systems learn like we do through trial and error learning, that requires exploration. That requires doing things and figuring out whether they're

good or bad. But when you try things out, there's also an opportunity to break things. So if we think of a water treatment plant, maybe increasing the amount of chemicals that's added to the water will help the agent learn that that's bad, but that would also be bad because we don't want people drinking water that has lots of chemicals in it. And the other unfortunate thing is, you that played well in Atari and the agent that did fusion control and the agent that was AlphaGo, all those agents are very, very different. And if you took one and applied it to the other situation, it wouldn't work at all. So researchers carefully tune and design these agents for

very bespoke deployments. And that's basically a non-starter when you think about moving things into the real world, because that's too slow. That's too expensive. We want general purpose solutions. That's probably the biggest reason why reinforcement methods are not really widely deployed. And so let's talk about water streaming, which is the application that really got me into all this. So this is the Norse Saskatchewan Glacier in the Rocky Mountains. That thing provides water for the Norse Saskatchewan River, which flows past Straighten Valley, where I started working on this project all the way to Edmonton where I'm sitting today. This is a huge watershed. You you can imagine all kinds of chemicals and actions by humans

and weather all along that long river affects this treatment process. But luckily water treatment, especially in Drayton Valley, but generally speaking is very, very simple. It's basically a two-stage process. You have water that comes in from a water source, in our case, the North Saskatchewan River, goes through a pretreatment phase where basically you add some chemicals that cause solids to clump in the water. And the reason you do that is because the next stage filtration, we wanna pull the clean water through and leave the solids there. And so if the solids are all clumped together, it's easier to filter them. So pre-treatment, filtration, and then into storage. Of course, there's a little bit of chlorine

and fluoride added after the filtration stage, but that's basically it. It's a basic two-stage procedure. And so this is the actual water-fuel implant in Drayton Valley, Alberta, and we can match that cartoon to this real system. So on the left, we have this really large tank, and that's where the water comes in. It's mixed slowly, and we add our are coagulant chemicals there to clump the solids together. And then on the right side, we have these two rectangular boxes with the yellow outline on the top. Those are the two filter banks that have two parallel streams and filters because if one goes down for maintenance, you still want to be able to make water. So very basic setup, two-stage process,

just like I described. And what's nice is as a control person, as an optimization person, I can step back and say, how can I make this plant better? And so if you look at some of the things in here, how fast that big tank mixes, how much chemicals we add, how do we control the cleaning of the filter? So this is called backwashing. So we literally run the water backwards through the filter that blasts all the gunk off the filter membrane, but that process is controlled by a bunch of set points, like how much air do you blow across the filter when you do that? And when does the backwashing start and how long does it last? All these decisions in these white bubbles here are process control variables

that were configured by engineers when the plant was commissioned. And so those could be better if they were changed with time. And of course, because the plant has changed with time, some of those set points are not ideal and we're actually wasting money, water, and chemical. And so this is not about replacing operators. Think of Canada, think of rural communities, specifically indigenous communities in the North. We have communities that have had boil water orders for the past 20 years, which is totally unacceptable. Those communities can get federal grant money to build mobile water treatment centers, but the issue is finding operators. Sometimes operators are unreliable, sometimes you just don't have someone in the community,

or sometimes you train someone and then they move to Edmonton to get a better job. And if you don't have those operators there every single day, the filters get fouled, we use lots of chemicals, and eventually there's just no water for the community because the treatment plant breaks down. And even in the case when we have skilled operators like in Dragon Valley, they're They're very, very busy and they need to focus on lots of different jobs and they can't spend time fiddling with those set points to optimize things. So they're busy. We want to allow them to focus on the key parts of their job, do the boring stuff in behind the scenes for them, and improve efficiency of the entire plant.

And so we made a startup to do exactly this. It's called IRO Core Technologies. We have 12 full-time employees, $7 million in VC funding, and currently we have three active deployments, Alberta. These are systems that are running 24-7, optimizing things in real time. And so at the Epcor wastewater treatment plant at Gold Bar, we have sour gas removal. So that's basically cleaning the air that comes out of the plants so it doesn't smell bad. This friend's 24-7 in Drayton Valley, we're controlling both chemical dosing in the pre-treatment stage and back washing to clean the filter. these again are running 24 seven all the time adjusting those set points up and

down, saving money, reducing the amount of water we're using and reducing the amount of chemicals we're using. And this is just the start. This formula, this general approach, can be applied across industrial control. You can think of desalination. You can think of oil and gas. You can think of food and beverage. All these things look similar and these kind of approaches based on reinforcement learning can be applied in these situations. So for the first time, we're moving AI systems out of research labs, out of video games, and into the real world where societal and monetary benefits are right there. And this is happening. Alberta is leading the charge on this. There's still fundamental research questions that remain,

and they're going to be tackled here at the U of A. And this is just a little picture of the number of researchers that worked specifically in reinforcement learning. and the key technology that my system is built on to show you the vast pipeline that we have access to. So hopefully that little teaser talk was useful and it will help you encourage you to look into this more. Thanks again.
